title: Alignment Inertia: Auditing the Durability of Training Data Influence Through Policy Override Resistance
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 23 Sep 2026]
    Title:Alignment Inertia: Auditing the Durability of Training Data Influence Through Policy Override Resistance
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Platform operators increasingly rely on system prompts and fine-tuning to govern model behavior, yet it remains unclear how reliably these interventions override behavior inherited from prior training. We propose Override Success Rate (OSR) and alignment inertia to measure when operator interventions succeed or fail to change prior behavior. We evaluate zero-shot prompting and LoRA fine-tuning across Llama and Mistral in medical misinformation and hate speech. Alignment inertia persists across both models but varies by model, domain, and policy direction. Notably, in Mistral's restrictive hate-speech condition, LoRA increased inertia by 46.5 percentage points, showing that fine-tuning can reinforce rather than override prior behavior. We also use TRAK to test whether inertia is associated with weaker adaptation signals. TRAK achieves AUC of at least 0.85 in 7 of 8 conditions and outperforms model confidence, TF-IDF similarity, and embedding similarity as a predictor of inertia. These results provide an operator-facing audit of where prior training constrains downstream model governance.

report.summary: New audit finds 'alignment inertia': prior training behavior often resists system prompts and LoRA fine-tuning, and fine-tuning can even strengthen unwanted behavior.
report.background: Platform operators increasingly treat system prompts and fine-tuning as policy levers: a model can be instructed to avoid medical misinformation or hate speech, or adapted with LoRA to follow new safety rules. This assumes later interventions reliably override behavior learned during pretraining. But models inherit patterns from massive web data, and prior work shows fine-tuning can degrade safety, resurrect forgotten knowledge, or cause unintended capability shifts. The paper studies this tension as 'alignment inertia,' asking when operator interventions genuinely change prior behavior and when they merely layer on top. It evaluates zero-shot prompting and LoRA fine-tuning on Llama and Mistral across medical misinformation and hate speech, measuring Override Success Rate. It also asks whether influence estimates can predict resistance. The results matter because safety, compliance, and platform governance often assume that policy changes at inference or fine-tuning time are durable, but inherited training influences may set hard boundaries on what operators can control.
key_points: The paper defines two metrics: Override Success Rate (OSR) and alignment inertia. OSR measures how often a prompt or fine-tune successfully changes a model's prior behavior, while inertia captures the residual resistance. This gives operators a quantitative audit rather than anecdotal evidence.

Across Llama and Mistral, alignment inertia persisted in both medical misinformation and hate speech tasks. However, its strength varied by model family, domain, and policy direction, meaning there is no single global fix for overriding prior behavior. Operators must test per context.

A striking result: in Mistral's restrictive hate-speech condition, LoRA fine-tuning increased inertia by 46.5 percentage points. Instead of overriding prior behavior, the adaptation reinforced it. This challenges the common assumption that fine-tuning is a stronger governance tool than prompting.

The authors use TRAK, an influence-estimation method, to test whether inertia correlates with weaker adaptation signals. TRAK achieved AUC of at least 0.85 in 7 of 8 conditions and beat model confidence, TF-IDF similarity, and embedding similarity as a predictor of inertia.

The work provides an operator-facing audit framework. It suggests that before deploying prompts or LoRA policies, teams should measure OSR and inertia on representative harms, and use influence estimates to flag cases where prior training may constrain downstream governance.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this paper challenges the default safety playbook: system prompts and fine-tuning are not guaranteed to overwrite inherited behavior. Model providers may need to document alignment inertia and offer per-domain override audits, while compliance teams should not assume that a policy layer equals durable behavioral change. Developers using Llama, Mistral, or similar open models should test interventions on target harms, compare prompting versus LoRA, and consider influence-based diagnostics like TRAK before release. It also implies that fine-tuning can backfire, reinforcing undesirable priors even when safety data is added. For regular users, the practical consequence is that AI assistants may continue to exhibit harmful biases or misinformation patterns despite visible policy updates. Safety claims based only on prompts or small fine-tunes deserve more scrutiny, and users should expect inconsistent behavior across domains and model versions.
report.tools: To follow up, explore TRAK (open-source influence estimation from the paper's authors), Hugging Face PEFT for LoRA experiments, and Captum or PyTorch influence-function libraries for diagnostics. Llama and Mistral model cards, plus evaluation harnesses like HELM or lm-evaluation-harness, can help reproduce domain-specific safety tests. For audit pipelines, combine prompt-injection tests, red-teaming datasets, and influence scores to flag alignment inertia before deployment.
